title: Bengal to move Supreme Court over Kolkata poll stay; Adhikari sets 13 November deadline
dek: The Chief Minister says he will appoint coordinators for all 209 wards if the High Court's bar on calling the KMC election stays in place.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
West Bengal's government will go to the Supreme Court against the Calcutta High Court order that has stopped the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) election from being called, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Friday. He also said that if the poll remains blocked, he will appoint "coordinators" for all 209 of the city's newly drawn wards after 13 November.

"We will approach the Supreme Court against this," Mr Adhikari told reporters on Friday evening. "I will wait till November 13. After that, I will appoint coordinators for all 209 wards." According to one report, the coordinators would act in place of councillors in their wards until an election is held. The state had not filed its appeal by Saturday morning.

## The High Court's order

On Friday a vacation division bench of Justice Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya and Justice Arjun Ray Mukherjee directed the State Election Commission not to issue a notification for the KMC election until a single-judge bench decides a pending challenge to the redrawing of the city's wards, according to reports of the order. On 29 October the single judge had declined to stay the process and asked the parties to file affidavits.

The petition challenges the state government's notification of 11 September, which increased the number of KMC wards from 144 to 209. It was filed by Dipu Das, a former CPI(M) councillor, and argued by senior advocate Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya.

The petitioners argued that the elected civic body was dissolved on 8 June, and that the new ward map was recommended by the administrator appointed to run the corporation, not by an elected board as the law requires. They also said the wards had been drawn on the basis of voter lists rather than population, and that the new boundaries amount to gerrymandering that favours one party.

For the state, Advocate General Surajit Nath Mitra argued that the government can redraw wards without a recommendation from the corporation, that the administrator exercises the corporation's powers while there is no elected board, and that the challenge had been brought at the last minute.

No date has been reported for the single judge's hearing. The High Court is on its puja vacation.

## What each side says

Mr Adhikari, whose Bharatiya Janata Party government took office after this year's Assembly election, dismissed the challenge. "Those who are destined to lose the election go to court, while those who are set to win focus on election preparations," he said. "We are preparing for the election. We are going to win."

Opposition parties welcomed the order. The CPI(M)'s Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya, who argued the case, welcomed it, as did former state Congress president Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury, who said the civic polls "will not be free and fair", according to reports. The state Congress had earlier written to West Bengal's Chief Electoral Officer alleging irregularities in the delimitation. The Trinamool Congress, which ran the corporation until June, and the State Election Commission had not commented publicly on the order by Saturday morning.

## Background

The KMC, which runs civic services for about 45 lakh people, has been without an elected board since June. Mr Adhikari had earlier promised a new board by 7 December, and reports had said the KMC and Howrah Municipal Corporation elections could be held this month or next. The state election body had already deferred publication of the final voter lists for the KMC and six other civic bodies.

## What happens next

The state is expected to file a petition in the Supreme Court in the coming days. Mr Adhikari's 13 November deadline falls before the High Court reopens after the vacation. Any appointment of ward coordinators without an election could itself be challenged in court.
